prompts.name: Progressive-Disclosure Spec & Harness Factorer
prompts.sprintRole: Refactor repository specs and harness resources into 50,000-, 30,000-, and 15,000-foot views so agents and developers load only the context required for the current question or workflow
prompts.useWhen: AGENTS.md, HARNESS.md, codebase maps, specifications, skills, workflows, registries, reports, or other agent resources have become duplicated or bloated and a simple repository question loads far more context than it needs.
prompts.inspectFirst: Current repository governance and precedence; agent/harness entrypoints; codebase/spec maps; workflow, capability, trigger, skill, artifact, and validator registries; actual context-loading behavior; document sizes; duplicated authority; representative 50k/30k/15k queries; existing context-engineering measurements when present.
prompts.expectedOutput: A measured progressive-disclosure architecture with one compact orientation layer, domain-level routing, workflow/spec-level detail, demand-loaded deep resources, canonical ownership links, executable context-budget checks, and before/after evidence that required behavior survives with less default context.
prompts.nextStep: Execute the highest-value safe factoring change now, run the repository's context/spec/harness validators plus the before/after load-budget check, and consume the new 50k entrypoint with one representative query before expanding deeper.
prompts.proofGate: A fresh user or agent can orient at 50k without loading deep implementation detail, select one domain at 30k, load only the triggered workflow/spec/skills at 15k, reach ground-level files on demand, preserve every unique authoritative rule, and show measured context reduction without a representative-task regression.
prompts.copyContent:
FACTOR THE REPOSITORY HARNESS AND SPECS FOR PROGRESSIVE DISCLOSURE. DO NOT TURN THIS INTO A DOCS REWRITE OR A SUMMARY-ONLY EXERCISE.

Repo: xyz_repo_or_path
Primary app or subsystem: xyz_app_or_subsystem
Known context pain, if any: xyz_context_bloat

MISSION
Make the repository understandable at three deliberate zoom levels while keeping deep implementation detail demand-loaded. Reduce default context, duplication, and token cost without deleting unique rules or weakening executable contracts. Change tracked files, validate the result, and measure the before/after context load.

ZOOM CONTRACT
1. 50,000 FT — ORIENTATION
A fresh user or agent should learn: what the app is for, major subsystems, canonical entrypoints, the few commands that matter, current proof/status boundaries, and where to drill down next. Target <= 1,000 approximate tokens of repo-specific material. This layer is a router, not an encyclopedia.

2. 30,000 FT — DOMAIN / CAPABILITY
After one domain is selected, load only that domain's responsibilities, inputs/outputs, dependencies, owning specs/contracts, artifacts, validators, and next drill-down links. Target <= 2,000 additional approximate tokens for the selected domain. Do not load unrelated domains.

3. 15,000 FT — WORKFLOW / SPEC
After one task or workflow is selected, load the exact workflow/spec, required skill procedure, relevant schema/registry records, validators, failure policy, and handoff/output contract. Target <= 4,000 additional approximate tokens for that selected workflow. Large code files, historical reports, full schemas, fixtures, and implementation detail remain on-demand.

These are default soft ceilings, not permission to omit required safety or correctness context. Exceed one only when the repository records why a smaller authoritative split would be unsafe or misleading. If tokenizer data is unavailable, measure characters/bytes and clearly mark token counts as estimates.

FACTOR BY RESPONSIBILITY
- `AGENTS.md`: governance, precedence, universal safety/operating law. Do not use it as the app encyclopedia.
- harness/spec entrypoint: compact 50k map and routing table.
- codebase/spec maps: 30k ownership and navigation, not copied workflow prose.
- workflow specs: trigger, inputs, outputs, dependencies, validator, failure policy, proof ceiling, and handoff.
- skills: repeatable procedure and judgment only; deterministic facts belong in code, schemas, registries, or validators.
- registries/schemas: machine-readable identity, ownership, routing, and contracts; prose should link to them instead of duplicating them.
- reports/history: evidence and current state, loaded only when the active task needs them.

REMOVE DEFAULT-BLOAT FAILURE MODES
Do not preload every skill, nested AGENTS file, tool schema, workflow, historical handoff, report, PR body, artifact manifest, or implementation file merely because it exists. Eliminate duplicated authority, repeated boilerplate, giant indexes that embed whole documents, and links that do not state when the target should be loaded. Preserve one canonical owner and lightweight references elsewhere.

MEASURE BEFORE MODIFYING
Inventory the harness/spec surfaces with path, purpose, owner, trigger/load condition, size, overlap, and consumer. Run at least three representative retrieval simulations:
- `What is this app and how is it organized?` — 50k
- `How does <one domain> work?` — 30k
- `How do I execute or change <one workflow/spec>?` — 15k
Record which files and approximate tokens/bytes each query requires before factoring.

IMPLEMENT, DON'T JUST RECOMMEND
Reuse existing repository patterns. Split or tighten bloated files, add compact indexes/metadata only where needed, replace duplicated prose with canonical references, add trigger/load metadata where routing is ambiguous, and update validators/tests so future changes cannot silently re-bloat the entry path. Do not move deterministic behavior into prose. Do not change product behavior merely to simplify documentation.

VALIDATE THE NEW INFORMATION ARCHITECTURE
Prove that:
- 50k answers do not require 15k resources;
- selecting one 30k domain excludes unrelated domains;
- 15k routing reaches every required spec, skill, validator, and artifact contract for the chosen workflow;
- no unique rule or authority disappeared during deduplication;
- links/IDs resolve;
- precedence remains explicit;
- representative tasks still succeed;
- measured default context falls meaningfully.
Fail closed on broken routing or lost authority.

DELIVER
Report the three-layer map, files factored, canonical owners, before/after context measurements, validation, commit/PR/merge state, and the exact first query/command that exercises the new 50k entrypoint. Keep the report itself concise: the goal is a quieter repository, not a larger explanation of why it is quiet.

prompts.name: Repository Glossary & Documentation Diet
prompts.sprintRole: Reduce conflicting repository prose by consolidating vocabulary into a lean glossary that points agents to executable sources of truth instead of restating implementation behavior
prompts.useWhen: Markdown and documentation have multiplied, agents cannot tell whether code or prose is current, terminology is inconsistent, or the repository needs a smaller durable vocabulary layer without losing unique operational rules.
prompts.inspectFirst: Repository governance and precedence; existing glossary or terminology surfaces; code, schemas, contracts, tests, validators, manifests, and registries that actually enforce behavior; documentation references/backlinks; runbooks or safety procedures that cannot safely be reduced to vocabulary entries.
prompts.expectedOutput: One existing or canonical glossary tightened into a compact vocabulary/navigation layer, redundant explanatory prose removed or collapsed where evidence proves it is duplicated, authoritative implementation paths linked per term, references repaired, and validation showing no unique rule or required operational procedure was lost.
prompts.nextStep: Mutate the highest-overlap documentation surface now, consolidate its reusable terms into the canonical glossary, repair references, and run the strongest repository documentation/harness/link plus behavior validators that prove the deleted prose was not an independent authority.
prompts.proofGate: Glossary entries define vocabulary rather than duplicate behavior; repository-specific precedence is preserved; executable code/contracts/schemas/tests/validators remain the implementation authority unless governance explicitly says otherwise; unique safety/runbook content is retained; stale duplicates are removed or clearly deprecated; and all affected validators/tests pass.
prompts.copyContent:
DIET THE REPOSITORY DOCUMENTATION DOWN TO A LEAN GLOSSARY AND AUTHORITATIVE POINTERS. EXECUTE THE REPOSITORY CHANGES; DO NOT JUST PROPOSE A DOC STRATEGY.

Repo: xyz_repo_or_path
Scope or subsystem: xyz_scope_or_resolve_from_context

MISSION
Reduce documentation bloat that causes agents to confuse stale prose with current implementation. Prefer one compact glossary for vocabulary and navigation. Keep behavior authoritative in code, schemas, contracts, registries, validators, and tests wherever the repository already enforces it there.

AUTHORITY FIRST
1. Read the repository's actual governance/precedence rules before deleting or demoting anything.
2. Inventory overlapping Markdown/docs and the executable surfaces they describe.
3. For each disputed behavior, determine the current enforceable owner from code/contracts/schemas/tests/validators rather than choosing the newest-looking prose.
4. Preserve non-glossary documentation only when it is a genuine operational input, safety/runbook procedure, external interface contract, or other unique authority that cannot safely be replaced by a pointer.

GLOSSARY CONTRACT
Use the existing glossary if one exists; otherwise create the repository's normal minimal glossary path. Each entry should contain only what helps an agent navigate: term, short meaning, authoritative path or owner, and an alias/status note only when useful. Keep definitions short. The glossary may explain vocabulary; it must not become a second specification of implementation behavior. Link to the executable owner instead of copying its rules.

IMPLEMENT THE DIET
Classify overlapping prose as KEEP-AUTHORITY, KEEP-OPERATIONAL, COLLAPSE-INTO-GLOSSARY, REPLACE-WITH-POINTER, or DELETE-REDUNDANT. Make the bounded changes now. Repair links, indexes, harness routes, and references that point to removed files. Do not create a new tutorial, architecture essay, migration diary, or duplicate policy merely to explain the cleanup. Do not change product behavior to make stale documentation true.

CONFLICT RULE
When narrative documentation disagrees with executable behavior, obey repository-specific precedence first. Absent a higher explicit authority, treat current code plus its contracts/tests/validators as implementation truth and update or remove the contradictory prose. Preserve uncertainty when executable evidence is incomplete instead of inventing reconciliation.

VALIDATE
Run the strongest practical documentation/harness validators, link/reference checks, targeted behavior tests for surfaces whose prose was removed, and `git diff --check`. Prove every deleted statement was duplicated, stale, or non-authoritative and that every unique rule still has one reachable owner.

DELIVER
Report the glossary path, files removed/collapsed/retained, authoritative owners established, validators run, commit/PR/merge state, and any remaining documentation that could not safely be reduced. Keep the final report compact; the purpose of this prompt is less repository text, not more.

prompts.name: Prompt Registry Prompt Adder
prompts.sprintRole: Harvest the full relevant current conversation into a bounded Prompt Kit contribution set, strengthening canonical owners first and using the repo helper only for genuinely missing identities
prompts.useWhen: The current chat contains one or more reusable prompt/workflow insights and the operator wants them represented in the Prompt Kit without restating prior context or creating overlapping prompt identities.
prompts.inspectFirst: The entire accessible current conversation relevant to the request, including earlier decisions, examples, corrections, constraints, and follow-ups; then current Triage main/PR floor, combined Prompt Kit ownership, focused semantic tests, and helper routing only when needed.
prompts.expectedOutput: A whole-chat contribution ledger that dispositions every material reusable insight, strengthens overlapping canonical owners, adds only genuinely missing bounded prompts through the helper, expands compatible utility beyond literal transcription, proves generated-site parity, and converges the exact green result to main.
prompts.nextStep: Sweep the whole relevant chat, build an insight-to-owner ledger, implement strengthen/add actions, then sweep the chat again for missed constraints or complementary utility before validation and mainline convergence.
prompts.proofGate: The immediate request is treated as the anchor rather than the context boundary; at least two deliberate context/coverage passes occur; every material reusable insight is dispositioned as STRENGTHEN, ADD, ALREADY COVERED, or OUT OF SCOPE; new identities are helper-allocated only after overlap review; compatible utility may be expanded without inventing requirements; and focused semantic plus exact-site-parity proof passes.
prompts.copyContent:
ADD OR STRENGTHEN PROMPT KIT PROMPTS FROM THE RELEVANT CHAT CONTEXT. THE CONTEXT IMMEDIATELY ABOVE THIS INSTRUCTION IS THE ANCHOR, NOT THE CONTEXT BOUNDARY. EXECUTE THE REPO WORK; DO NOT ASK ME TO RESTATE CONTEXT THAT IS ALREADY ACCESSIBLE.

CANONICAL REPO
`EndeavorEverlasting/web-excel-repair-triage`

MISSION
Turn the current request plus earlier relevant chat decisions into the smallest complete Prompt Kit contribution set. Recover approved/rejected wording, examples, corrections, constraints, related ideas, and prior definitions that materially affect the request. Strengthen canonical owners before creating identities. Use the repo helper for genuinely new prompts; do not manually rediscover deterministic registry mechanics.

1. WHOLE-CHAT HARVEST — PASS 1
- Read the current request, then traverse earlier accessible context for the same use case and dependencies. Include recoverable pasted/generated context or history when available; ignore unrelated history.
- Build `insight | current owner | action | proof` with action STRENGTHEN / ADD / ALREADY COVERED / OUT OF SCOPE.
- No material insight may silently disappear. Do not ask the user to repeat recoverable context.

2. OWNER MAP BEFORE NEW IDS
Search the combined Prompt Kit for an exact, adjacent, or materially overlapping prompt. Compare trigger, mission, scope, and closure—not title alone.
- STRENGTHEN when an owner has the core use case but lacks a compatible context, failure, live-proof, iteration, or usability rule.
- ADD only for genuinely missing bounded behavior with a distinct trigger and closure condition.
- ALREADY COVERED requires concrete current prompt evidence.
Do not create a second identity because alternate wording sounds attractive.

3. COMPLEMENT — DO NOT MERELY TRANSCRIBE
Preserve explicit user intent and terminology, then expand compatible utility revealed by chat/repo evidence: useful failure states, entrypoints, proof levels, context recovery, user-only gates, iteration, discoverability, or integration seams. Expansion must make the requested workflow more executable, reusable, testable, or failure-resistant. Do not invent unrelated requirements or universal checklists.

4. IMPLEMENT THE CONTRIBUTION SET
For STRENGTHEN, edit the canonical source and closest focused regression.
For ADD:
- choose the closest existing registry/profile; run `python scripts/prompt_registry_ops.py inspect` only if routing is unclear;
- draft semantic fields only; Do NOT set id, seq, or copySheet;
- run `python scripts/prompt_registry_ops.py add --input <draft.json> --registry <existing_registry_id>`;
- let the helper allocate identity, reject obvious duplicates, inject shared policy, rebuild the site, prove parity, and roll back registry/site writes if validation fails.
Multiple genuinely distinct prompts may be added from one chat; do not collapse them into a super-prompt merely to keep one identity.

5. WHOLE-CHAT HARVEST — PASS 2
After implementation, traverse the relevant context again from the opposite direction. Look for missed `also`, `another`, `we skipped`, `strengthen`, `live`, `regression`, `prototype`, corrections/examples, referenced sources, earlier accepted definitions, and neighboring owners that should be strengthened to avoid overlap. Update the ledger and close concrete gaps. Stop at a bounded fixed point; do not stop at the first helper receipt or manufacture passes with no new evidence.

6. FOCUSED PROOF + CONVERGENCE
Add or extend the closest focused semantic assertion the generic helper cannot prove. Verify new prompts remain distinct and strengthened prompts retain their original role. Run `python scripts/prompt_registry_ops.py validate`, focused tests, applicable language/order/discovery checks, generated-site `--check`, and `git diff --check`. Refresh the default-branch floor before final proof; reconcile moved dependencies; then merge the exact green authorized head into main.

FAIL-CLOSED
If routing is ambiguous, inspect once. If a contract mismatch names an owner/helper/builder, inspect only that surface. Do not fall back to loading the entire Prompt Kit architecture, guess identities, bypass parity, weaken a validator, or make the operator a context courier/test runner.

DELIVER
Keep it compact: contribution ledger; strengthened IDs/names; new helper receipts; focused semantic assertion results; prompt count/parity; validation; commit/PR/merge; resulting main SHA; exact blocker if any.

prompts.inspectFirst: Current Prompt Kit registry schema and renderer; local Favorites and portability/storage contracts; search/filter/category/color behavior; existing import/export helpers; stable-origin browser storage; mobile/accessibility patterns; generated-site boundary; security rules for untrusted JSON and pasted text; versioning/migration conventions.

prompts.name: Multi-Tier Cache Architecture & Invalidation Hardener
prompts.sprintRole: Design and implement a measured cache architecture across browser, edge, gateway, application L1, distributed L2, and database layers with explicit invalidation, stampede, penetration, avalanche, coherence, privacy, and failure controls
prompts.useWhen: An application needs lower latency, reduced origin/database load, offline or repeated-read efficiency, or production cache reliability and the correct layer, invalidation method, multi-tier behavior, and failure protections are not yet explicit.
prompts.inspectFirst: Request/data flow; read/write ratios; consistency and freshness requirements; existing browser/CDN/proxy/app/distributed/database caches; data sensitivity; latency and origin-load measurements; current key design/TTL/eviction; mutation/event path; Redis/Memcached or equivalent infrastructure; failure incidents and observability.
prompts.expectedOutput: A measured cache map and implemented policy with justified cache layers, key/version scheme, TTL and active invalidation, L1/L2 coherence, stampede/penetration/avalanche mitigations, failure/privacy controls, observability, tests/benchmarks, and a proof ceiling that distinguishes synthetic cache correctness from production latency.
prompts.nextStep: Prototype the highest-value cache tier on one representative hot read, benchmark hit/miss/stale paths against the uncached baseline, inject expiry/concurrency/mutation failures, and refine invalidation and protection controls before expanding coverage.
prompts.proofGate: Every cached value has an owner, freshness target, key/version, invalidation path, capacity/eviction policy, security classification, and miss/failure behavior; multi-tier coherence is explicit; stampede, penetration, and avalanche cases are tested; cache loss degrades safely; metrics expose hits/misses/staleness/origin load; and claimed latency gains come from measurements in the relevant runtime.
prompts.copyContent:
DESIGN AND HARDEN THE APPLICATION'S CACHE ARCHITECTURE. TREAT CACHING AS A CONSISTENCY AND FAILURE-SYSTEM PROBLEM, NOT JUST A SPEED SWITCH.

Repo: xyz_repo_or_path
Application/request path: xyz_request_path
Primary latency/load/freshness problem: xyz_cache_problem

MISSION
Reduce repeated-work latency and origin load without creating stale, insecure, incoherent, or failure-prone data paths. Start from measured traffic/data behavior, choose only cache layers that earn their complexity, implement invalidation before declaring success, and validate concurrency/failure cases before expanding the cache footprint.

1. MAP THE MULTI-TIER CACHE HIERARCHY
Inspect every layer that can currently cache or retain a response/value:
- Client browser: HTTP cache headers and intentionally cache-like local state; distinguish durable LocalStorage/IndexedDB state from a cache unless it has freshness/invalidation semantics.
- Edge/CDN: Cloudflare, Fastly, or equivalent geo-distributed response/static/SSR caching.
- Reverse proxy/gateway: Nginx, API Gateway, or service-mesh response caching.
- Application L1: in-process memory, framework cache, Guava/Caffeine, `sync.Map`, or equivalent—fast and network-free but isolated to one process/instance.
- Distributed L2: Redis, Memcached, or equivalent—network hop, shared state across application instances.
- Database internal: buffer pools, materialized/query/result caches where the database actually supports them.
Do not assume a latency number from a diagram is universal. Treat sub-microsecond L1 and low-millisecond L2 figures as conceptual expectations only; benchmark the actual runtime, network, serialization, payload, and contention path.

2. DECIDE WHAT DESERVES TO BE CACHED
For each candidate record: source of truth, read/write ratio, recomputation cost, request fan-out, acceptable staleness, cardinality, size, sensitivity, tenant/user scope, and failure consequence. Reject caching when invalidation/security complexity exceeds the measured benefit. Define whether cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-behind, request memoization/single-flight, stale-while-revalidate, or no cache best matches the data path.

3. INVALIDATION: TACKLE STALE DATA EXPLICITLY
TTL / PASSIVE INVALIDATION
- Expire keys after a bounded interval when slight eventual consistency is acceptable.
- Choose TTL from freshness/risk evidence, not a round-number habit.
- Use for high-churn or low-risk data such as weather-like feeds, counters, derived views, or other records where bounded staleness is acceptable.

EVENT-DRIVEN / ACTIVE INVALIDATION
- On authoritative mutation, publish a targeted invalidation/update event from the owning transaction/event path.
- Use database events, outbox, Change Data Capture, Debezium, or the repository's existing event bus when correctness requires rapid revocation.
- Favor this for permissions, authentication/session state, financial/account balances, entitlements, and similarly sensitive correctness paths.
- Design for duplicate, delayed, reordered, or lost events; do not assume CDC is magic coherence.

CACHE VERSIONING / KEY NAMESPACING
- Include schema/dataset/tenant/profile version in key names such as `user:v2:1049` when a version bump should invalidate a whole logical generation.
- Prefer namespace/version rollover over an expensive global flush when practical.
- Define key encoding, tenant isolation, canonical serialization, maximum key/value size, and migration/old-version retirement.

4. PREVENT PRODUCTION CACHE FAILURE MODES
CACHE STAMPEDE / THUNDERING HERD
Problem: a hot key expires and many concurrent requests miss at once, overwhelming the origin.
Controls: per-key mutex or distributed lock, single-flight request coalescing, stale-while-revalidate, bounded lock timeout, and probabilistic early expiration/XFetch-style refresh where justified. Never make waiting callers deadlock behind a failed recompute.

CACHE PENETRATION
Problem: repeated requests for nonexistent/invalid IDs bypass useful cached data and hammer the origin.
Controls: input validation, negative caching of known-missing results with a short TTL, Bloom filter when the key universe and false-positive tradeoff justify it, plus abuse/rate controls where traffic is malicious. Never negative-cache authorization-sensitive absence longer than its correctness window.

CACHE AVALANCHE
Problem: many keys share the same expiry instant and fall through together.
Control: TTL jitter—add bounded random variation around the base TTL—plus staggered warming/preload where evidence supports it. Test a batch-expiry scenario rather than merely adding randomness.

HOT KEYS / CAPACITY / EVICTION
Measure memory, item count, hit rate by key class, payload sizes, hot-key concentration, eviction rate, fragmentation, connection pool saturation, and serialization cost. Choose eviction policy and memory ceilings deliberately. Do not let one tenant or unbounded key dimension exhaust shared cache capacity.

5. L1 + L2 COHERENCE
When using multi-tier caching, define the exact read path, write/invalidation path, and failure order. A typical cache-aside path may check L1 -> L2 -> origin, then populate outward, but mutation must prevent a stale L1 from surviving after L2 was corrected. Use version tokens, short L1 TTLs, pub/sub invalidation, request version checks, or another explicit coherence mechanism. State which layer is authoritative: normally none of the caches are.

6. REDIS VS MEMCACHED / TECHNOLOGY CHOICE
Choose from workload requirements rather than popularity. Compare data structures/atomic operations, persistence/replication needs, clustering, eviction behavior, memory efficiency, multi-key semantics, scripting/transactions, operational maturity, client support, observability, and failure behavior. Use a simpler cache when simple key/value eviction is genuinely enough; use richer coordination primitives only when the system needs them.

7. SECURITY, PRIVACY, AND FAILURE DEGRADATION
Never cache secrets or sensitive cross-user data without an explicit tenant/user key boundary and retention policy. Encrypt transport where required. Prevent cache poisoning and untrusted key construction. Decide whether a cache outage should fail open to origin, fail closed, serve stale, or shed load; bound origin fallback so losing the cache does not automatically take down the database. Circuit-break or rate-limit fallback when necessary.

8. OBSERVABILITY AND MEASURED PROOF
Instrument hit/miss/stale rates, latency by hit layer, recomputation time, lock contention, early refreshes, invalidation lag/failures, negative-cache hits, evictions, memory, error rate, origin/database load, and cache-outage fallback. Measure p50/p95/p99 where traffic warrants it. A high hit rate is not success if stale reads, latency, or memory cost are unacceptable.

9. PROTOTYPE AND FAULT-INJECT
Start with one representative hot read and one mutation path. Compare uncached baseline, L1-only, L2-only, and multi-tier candidates only when each is plausible. Then test concurrent expiry, missing IDs, batch expiry, delayed invalidation, cache restart/loss, stale L1 after mutation, Redis/Memcached timeout, and origin overload protection. Keep the simplest candidate that meets the measured requirement.

DELIVER
Implement the smallest justified cache policy, key/version/invalidation code, focused tests, benchmark or load fixture, observability, and configuration. Report layer map, consistency model, invalidation rules, stampede/penetration/avalanche controls, measured baseline/candidate results, failure behavior, security boundary, files/commit/PR, and remaining production-proof gates.

prompts.name: Prototype-Measure-Refine Delivery Loop
prompts.sprintRole: Make iterative prototyping a disciplined delivery loop: build the smallest real candidate, measure it against stable acceptance criteria, critique observable gaps, preserve evidence, refine deliberately, and only promote a candidate to final after integration-quality proof
prompts.useWhen: The desired feature, interface, artifact, architecture, workflow, or automation has meaningful unknowns and quality improves when an agent builds working prototypes, checks itself against evidence, compares alternatives, and refines repeatedly before final delivery.
prompts.inspectFirst: User outcome and acceptance criteria; current working behavior; highest-risk unknowns; existing prototypes/branches/artifacts; reusable implementation patterns; validators/tests; performance/accessibility/security constraints; feedback already supplied; time/cost budget and irreversible actions. When interaction flow is the uncertainty, inspect the exact terminal user goal, current step/keystroke sequence, focus/search/filter/selection state, completion feedback, and any existing semantic usage/preference event owner before prototyping a new UI path.
prompts.expectedOutput: A bounded sequence of increasingly faithful working candidates with hypothesis/acceptance criteria, evidence from each iteration, explicit keep/revise/discard decisions, preserved last-known-good state, final cleanup of prototype debt, and a release candidate that passes the same stable acceptance rubric plus integration regressions. For flow-focused iterations, include before/after journey evidence that distinguishes useful terminal actions from redundant intermediate screens and, when personalization is requested, measures semantic completions rather than views or focus events.
prompts.nextStep: Build the smallest real prototype that tests the highest-risk assumption, measure it against the fixed acceptance rubric, record the concrete gap, preserve the last-known-good candidate, and immediately execute the next justified refinement until the release-candidate gate is met or an exact blocker is proven.
prompts.proofGate: Each iteration changes a testable assumption rather than producing cosmetic churn; candidates are evaluated against stable criteria; evidence is recorded without inventing success; regressions and discarded paths are visible; no prototype is mislabeled final; the final candidate removes temporary stubs/debt, passes focused and integration validation, and satisfies the user outcome at the highest proof level available. When the hypothesis is interaction flow, orthogonal UI state is preserved unless the action explicitly owns it, the candidate reaches the terminal user goal without redundant steps, and any usage metric counts a meaningful completion exactly once rather than treating panel opens or views as intent.
prompts.copyContent:
DELIVER THE USER'S REQUEST THROUGH DISCIPLINED PROTOTYPE -> MEASURE -> REFINE ITERATIONS. DO NOT JUMP FROM IDEA TO FINAL CLAIM IN ONE UNCHECKED PASS.

Repo or workspace: xyz_repo_or_path
Target outcome: xyz_user_outcome
Known constraints: xyz_constraints_or_resolve_from_context

MISSION
Use prototypes as deliberate learning instruments on the way to the final result. Build working slices, check each candidate against stable acceptance criteria and observable evidence, preserve what works, discard what does not, and raise fidelity step by step. Iteration is not permission for endless churn: every loop must reduce a named uncertainty or close a measured gap.

1. LOCK THE OUTCOME BEFORE ITERATING
Recover the user outcome, non-negotiable constraints, owned/forbidden scope, and completion proof. Convert vague quality goals into a compact acceptance rubric that remains stable across candidates. If the rubric changes because the user changed the request or evidence disproved an assumption, record that change explicitly so later prototypes are not judged against moving goalposts silently.

2. TARGET THE HIGHEST-RISK UNKNOWN FIRST
Do not prototype the easy decorative parts while the core uncertainty remains untouched. Identify the assumption most likely to force rework: feasibility, data shape, interaction flow, architecture, performance, integration, compatibility, safety, or user comprehension. Build the smallest REAL end-to-end slice that tests it. A prototype may be narrow; it may not fake the very behavior being evaluated.

PROTOTYPE LADDER
Use only as much fidelity as the uncertainty requires:
- Spike: throwaway experiment proving/disproving feasibility or an API/format assumption.
- Functional prototype: smallest real user path with genuine state/data flow and focused tests.
- Integrated candidate: uses real repository owners/contracts and interacts with neighboring systems.
- Release candidate: feature-complete for the agreed scope, temporary scaffolding removed, regression/security/accessibility/performance gates run where relevant.
- Final: exact accepted candidate integrated into canonical state with evidence and no known release-blocking gap.
Do not present a prototype as final merely because the happy path looks convincing.

3. RUN THE ITERATION LOOP
For every meaningful iteration use the same explicit cycle:
HYPOTHESIS -> BUILD -> MEASURE -> CRITIQUE -> DECIDE
- HYPOTHESIS: name the uncertainty and what observation would count as better/worse.
- BUILD: mutate the smallest real surface that tests it; reuse current patterns instead of spawning parallel architecture without cause.
- MEASURE: run the relevant test, validator, benchmark, visual check, fixture, user-flow exercise, or artifact comparison.
- CRITIQUE: compare observable output to the acceptance rubric. State gaps, regressions, and tradeoffs; do not manufacture private chain-of-thought or vague self-praise.
- DECIDE: KEEP, REFINE, COMPARE, or DISCARD with a concrete reason and next executable action.
Then execute the next justified loop immediately when safe work remains.

3A. WHEN USER FLOW IS THE UNKNOWN — MEASURE THE JOURNEY, NOT THE SCREEN
When the risky assumption is interaction flow, write the actual sequence from entrypoint to terminal user value before changing UI. Track steps/keystrokes, focus changes, search/filter/selection state, intermediate panels, completion feedback, and destructive resets. Do not accept `panel opened` or `detail visible` as success when the user's real goal is to copy, execute, submit, compare, navigate, or otherwise use the object. Prefer the shortest understandable route that preserves safety and discoverability.

Test composed sequences, not only isolated controls. A control that owns visibility must not erase an active query, selection, or unrelated state unless that destructive transition is part of its explicit contract. If the user requests personalization or a most-used surface, measure semantic completion events such as successful copy/execute/export rather than hover, focus, panel-open, or detail-view noise; derive preference views from that canonical event owner instead of hard-coded ordering.

4. PRESERVE THE LAST KNOWN-GOOD STATE
Iteration must not destroy evidence. Use branch/worktree isolation, commits, versioned artifacts, fixtures, screenshots, manifests, hashes, or repository-native checkpoints as appropriate. Preserve the last known-good candidate before a risky redesign. Never use destructive cleanup merely to make a prototype floor look clean. Make it possible to compare or roll back candidates.

5. COMPARE ALTERNATIVES FAIRLY
When two approaches are genuinely plausible and the choice matters, build bounded competing prototypes rather than arguing abstractly. Run both through the SAME acceptance rubric and representative data/workload. Compare correctness first, then user experience, complexity, maintainability, performance, cost, security, and reversibility as relevant. Do not keep multiple production paths after the evidence selects one unless redundancy itself is a requirement.

6. USE FEEDBACK WITHOUT TURNING THE USER INTO THE TEST RUNNER
Automate what can be proven deterministically. Ask for human/user feedback when visual taste, workflow comfort, domain judgment, or acceptance genuinely cannot be settled by tests. Present a concrete candidate and a focused decision, not an unfinished pile of options. Incorporate already-given feedback into the next iteration instead of repeatedly asking the same question.

7. BOUND THE LOOP
Define a time/cost/iteration budget when experimentation could sprawl. Continue while each iteration closes a material gap. Stop or escalate when:
- the acceptance rubric is satisfied at the required proof level;
- further improvement is cosmetic and outside scope;
- the next uncertainty requires unavailable credentials, protected runtime, hardware, human approval, or external evidence;
- two or more iterations produce no material improvement, signaling that the hypothesis/architecture must be reconsidered rather than endlessly tweaked.

8. REMOVE PROTOTYPE DEBT BEFORE FINAL
A release candidate must not quietly ship throwaway scaffolding. Remove or disposition hard-coded fixture paths, fake data, temporary feature flags, duplicate implementations, debug UI/logging, placeholder copy, TODO-only correctness gaps, unsafe bypasses, dead experiments, and one-off scripts that are not part of the durable contract. Promote any useful prototype helper into the repository's normal owner with tests; delete redundant alternatives only when preservation rules allow it.

9. FINAL PROOF IS STRICTER THAN PROTOTYPE PROOF
Re-run the focused acceptance checks on the final candidate plus the strongest practical integration/regression/build/static/security/accessibility/performance gates relevant to the change. Compare final output to the user's original outcome, not merely to the previous prototype. Record skipped gates and proof ceilings exactly. Commit, push, review, and integrate the exact validated candidate when authorized.

DELIVER
Report the prototype ladder actually used, the hypothesis and evidence for each material iteration, discarded/retained approaches, last-known-good preservation, final cleanup, validation, commit/PR/merge state, remaining proof gaps, and the canonical artifact/path that represents the final candidate. Keep the report concise enough that the iterations produce learning rather than documentation bloat.

prompts.name: Prompt Semantic Hardener & Principle Integrator
prompts.sprintRole: Audit one existing Prompt Kit prompt against stronger compatible principles already proven elsewhere in the current registry, then harden that same canonical prompt without duplicating shared policy or changing its identity unnecessarily.
prompts.useWhen: An existing prompt still works but is older, thinner, or semantically weaker than newer Prompt Kit patterns; for example P03 may need compatible principles now present in P07, P13, P48, P76, P83, P84, P85, or shared policy owners.
prompts.inspectFirst: Current main/PR/evidence floor; target prompt in both raw and effective registry form; target registry/profile owner; shared prompt policies; the smallest set of stronger related prompts; target-focused tests; generated Prompt Kit parity and current review/CI evidence.
prompts.expectedOutput: The same target prompt identity hardened through a documented principle-applicability matrix, minimal compatible semantic edits, focused regression proof, bounded source size, exact generated-site parity, and integration to main when authorized.
prompts.nextStep: Select the named target prompt, compare its raw and effective behavior to the strongest relevant peers and shared owners, apply only compatible missing principles, add focused semantic regression proof, validate exact site parity, and converge the exact green head to main.
prompts.proofGate: The target retains its identity and primary role; every added principle has a current donor or policy owner plus an applicability reason; inherited policy is not recopied into raw source; incompatible or irrelevant principles are rejected explicitly; old required semantics and new hardening semantics are both tested; raw prompt size stays bounded; generated-site parity and exact-head integration proof pass.
prompts.copyContent:
HARDEN ONE EXISTING PROMPT USING THE STRONGEST COMPATIBLE PRINCIPLES ALREADY PROVEN ELSEWHERE IN THE CURRENT PROMPT KIT. MODIFY THE CANONICAL TARGET; DO NOT CREATE A DUPLICATE PROMPT JUST TO IMPROVE IT.

Target prompt: xyz_prompt_id_or_name_or_resolve_from_immediately_preceding_context
Specific weakness, if known: xyz_known_gap_or_infer_from_evidence

MISSION
Make an existing prompt materially stronger without turning it into a collage of every rule in the Prompt Kit. Preserve the target's identity, role, registry/profile, and useful semantics. Find stronger current patterns, decide which actually apply, harden the target source and focused tests, rebuild through canonical machinery, and integrate the exact validated result.

1. RESOLVE CURRENT TRUTH
Work from current repository/provider truth, not remembered prompt text. Resolve the current target prompt, its owning raw registry record, its effective built form, current shared policy owners, focused tests, generated site, and overlapping prompt/PR work. If the prompt identity already has an owning hardening branch or PR, reuse or repair that owner instead of opening a competing lane. Refresh again immediately before final exact-head conclusions; if main, the target, a donor, or a shared owner moves materially, reclassify affected evidence and rerun the applicability/validation decisions it could change.

2. RAW VS EFFECTIVE PROMPT
Read both forms before editing. The raw registry record owns prompt-specific semantics. The effective prompt may also contain injected shared policy. Separate those layers so you do not paste global actionability, repository-freshness, integration, or other builder-owned boilerplate back into the source record. If a desired behavior is already inherited and effective, count it as present unless the raw prompt has a direct-consumer reason to carry a small prompt-specific version.

3. HARVEST ONLY RELEVANT DONORS
Inspect the smallest useful set of stronger current prompts and shared owners that overlap the target's job. Candidate principles may include: fresh repository/evidence floors; exact artifact or commit identity; evidence-version invalidation; bounded implement/validate/critique iteration; continuous acceptance-gate progression without status spinning; autonomous agent work with a user-only escalation gate; fail-closed safety; source-of-truth precedence; proof ceilings; existing-work reuse and convergence; progressive disclosure/context restraint; interruption recovery from durable checkpoints; preservation of dirty or separately owned work; explicit acceptance criteria; anti-fabrication boundaries; canonical-owner selection instead of duplicated doctrine; and focused semantic regression. Do not assume every strong principle belongs in every target.

4. BUILD A PRINCIPLE APPLICABILITY MATRIX
Before mutation, record a compact matrix with one row per candidate principle:
- principle
- current donor or canonical policy owner
- already present in RAW, EFFECTIVE, BOTH, or ABSENT
- target-specific gap or failure mode
- COMPATIBLE, INCOMPATIBLE, or NOT NEEDED
- minimal source change, shared-owner change, or NO CHANGE
- focused proof that will show the decision is correct
Use repository semantics and the target's purpose to decide applicability. A newer prompt is evidence of a pattern, not automatic authority over an unrelated prompt.

5. HARDEN THE CANONICAL TARGET
Patch the existing prompt record rather than renumbering or cloning it. Update only the semantic fields that need strengthening: usually inspectFirst, sprintRole, expectedOutput, nextStep, proofGate, copyContent, or keywords. Keep profile/color/category and identity stable unless the repository has a separate explicit reason to change them. Reuse concise named concepts instead of copying whole donor sections. If the correct fix belongs in a shared policy or builder-owned contract, change that owner only when the requested scope genuinely applies to all affected prompts and run the broader regressions that ownership requires.

6. P03 REFERENCE CASE
When P03 / Repository Evidence + First Sprint Executor is the target, explicitly compare its older evidence-harvest/execution semantics with applicable current principles from P07 (iterative autonomous repo execution and convergence), P13 (bounded self-improvement and evidence critique), P48 (fresh subject/evidence pinning and stale-proof invalidation where certification-like proof is claimed), P76 (progressive disclosure and context restraint), P83 (treat completion/handoff claims as hypotheses until verified), P84 (continuous acceptance-gate progression, green-slice convergence, anti-spin, and resumable checkpoints), P85 (canonical-owner hardening, focused failure regressions, and avoiding duplicated doctrine), and the current shared policies. Adopt only principles that strengthen P03's actual discovery-plus-first-sprint job; do not transform P03 into P07, P13, P48, P76, P83, P84, or P85.

7. ANTI-BLOAT / ANTI-CARGO-CULT GATE
Reject changes whose only rationale is 'another prompt has this.' Do not copy every strong rule into every prompt. Prefer inherited shared policy, compact references, or one target-specific sentence when they provide equivalent enforcement. Remove duplicated source prose introduced by the hardening pass. If the raw target grows materially, justify each added block against a concrete gap and look for a smaller formulation before accepting it.

8. SEMANTIC REGRESSION PROOF
Extend the closest existing focused test. Prove the target still retains its prior defining behavior and now contains the newly selected semantics. Add a negative/boundary assertion when useful so the test also proves the target did not absorb an incompatible donor role. Check the raw-source size or other anti-bloat boundary when practical. Do not replace semantic proof with a screenshot or generated-site presence test alone.

9. VALIDATE AND ITERATE
Run the target registry/helper validation, focused semantic test, applicable prompt-language/order/discovery/build checks, exact generated-site parity, and patch hygiene. Inspect the resulting diff and evidence for one deliberate second pass. If the hardening introduced duplicated policy, identity drift, weakened old behavior, stale generated output, an untested principle, unnecessary size growth, or a newly moved donor/base, repair it and rerun affected checks. Stop iterating only when no practical in-scope semantic improvement or regression remains.

DELIVER
Report the target prompt identity, donor/applicability decisions, semantic fields changed, focused proof, rejected incompatible principles, raw-size impact, helper/builder or registry validation, generated-site parity, commit/PR/merge state, and resulting main SHA or exact blocker. Keep the report compact. The success condition is a stronger prompt with clearer proof, not a larger prompt.

prompts.name: Bidirectional Use-Case Hook & Repository Route Builder
prompts.sprintRole: Wire one supported repository use case into the existing harness so agents and developers can traverse from user intent to canonical implementation and from any participating implementation artifact back to its owning capability, originating intent, related resources, and proof.
prompts.useWhen: A repository has useful scripts, manifests, agents, skills, validators, or workflows but people still need tribal knowledge or filenames to find the right execution path, or when implementation files cannot explain which use case owns them and what proves them correct.
prompts.inspectFirst: Current repository governance and precedence; existing 50k/30k/15k routing entrypoints; trigger, capability, workflow, skill, manifest, composition, artifact, validator, and agent registries; the requested use case; its current implementation and proof surfaces; nearby routes that may already own the intent.
prompts.expectedOutput: One bounded bidirectional route integrated into existing repository routing owners: intent to trigger/capability/workflow/implementation/artifact/proof, plus reverse ownership from participating resources back to capability and user intent, with machine-checkable link resolution and representative traversal proof.
prompts.nextStep: Select the requested use case, trace its current forward and reverse discoverability, wire only the missing edges into existing canonical routing owners, add the smallest validator/regression that proves both traversals, and exercise the route from intent and from one implementation artifact.
prompts.proofGate: A fresh agent given only the desired use case can reach the canonical implementation and proof without already knowing filenames, and an agent landing on a participating script, manifest, validator, prompt, workflow, or capability record can determine why it exists, what capability owns it, which user intent leads there, what else participates, and what proves the path works; every referenced edge resolves without duplicate ownership or a new parallel registry family.
prompts.copyContent:
BUILD BIDIRECTIONAL USE-CASE HOOKS INTO THE EXISTING REPOSITORY HARNESS. EXECUTE THE ROUTING WORK; DO NOT REPLACE THE HARNESS OR WRITE AN ARCHITECTURE ESSAY.

Repo: xyz_repo_or_path
Desired use case: xyz_user_intent_or_workflow
Known entrypoint or implementation, if any: xyz_optional_path_or_id

MISSION
Make the desired use case easy to traverse without tribal knowledge. A supported workflow should be discoverable by intent, and every participating implementation resource should be able to point back to why it exists and who owns it. Treat the repository as a navigable graph of intent, capability, execution, artifacts, and proof rather than a pile of filenames.

THIS PROMPT HAS A NARROW JOB
Do not rebuild the whole harness merely because routing is incomplete. Harness Builder may create or repair general harness infrastructure; Progressive-Disclosure factoring may reduce default context. This prompt wires one bounded use case into the current routing system and repairs only the routing seams required to make that path deterministic. Reuse current governance, registries, manifests, maps, skills, agents, workflows, and validators before inventing another owner.

BIDIRECTIONAL ROUTE CONTRACT
Forward traversal must resolve the shortest authoritative path that actually exists in the repository:
USER INTENT -> TRIGGER / HOOK -> CAPABILITY -> SKILL OR WORKFLOW CONTRACT -> IMPLEMENTATION -> EXPECTED ARTIFACT -> VALIDATOR / PROOF.

Reverse traversal must work from every participating implementation-side resource:
SCRIPT / MANIFEST / VALIDATOR / PROMPT / WORKFLOW / CAPABILITY RECORD -> OWNING CAPABILITY -> ORIGINATING USER INTENT / TRIGGER -> RELATED PARTICIPANTS -> PROOF.

Do not require every repository to use those exact filenames or document types. Map the concepts onto the repository's existing owners. Stable IDs and machine-readable registry edges are preferred where the repository already has them. Human-facing maps should explain when to follow an edge, not duplicate the target's full contents.

DISCOVER BEFORE WRITING
1. Resolve current governance and instruction precedence.
2. Start from the supplied use case in plain language. Search existing triggers, capabilities, workflows, skills, agents, manifests, composition graphs, artifact registries, validators, and implementation helpers for an obvious owner.
3. Trace the current route as far as it works. Record each edge as RESOLVES, AMBIGUOUS, MISSING, STALE, or DUPLICATE.
4. Start again from at least one concrete implementation-side resource already participating in the use case and trace backward.
5. If an existing route already provides both traversals, strengthen its proof instead of creating a duplicate hook.

BUILD THE SMALLEST MISSING ROUTING SEAMS
Use existing canonical routing surfaces. Add or repair only what is necessary to make the path deterministic, such as:
- intent aliases or trigger records that recognize the real operator wording;
- capability ownership IDs and links;
- workflow/skill references that state when they load;
- implementation metadata or nearby registry records that identify the owning capability;
- artifact and validator links that expose the proof boundary;
- lightweight backlinks so an agent arriving at an implementation resource can recover the owning route.

Prefer registry/schema fields and validators over repeated prose when the repository already treats routing as machine-readable. Do not move deterministic behavior into Markdown. Do not create a second capabilities registry, trigger family, skill catalog, composition graph, or artifact registry merely to support this use case.

PROGRESSIVE-DISCLOSURE COMPATIBILITY
Keep the route cheap to enter. The 50k/orientation layer should identify the domain or routing entrypoint, the 30k layer should reveal the capability and its dependencies, and the task/workflow layer should load the exact skill, implementation, artifacts, and validator required. Do not preload every participating document merely to prove that links exist. Route first; load detail on demand.

INTENT OVER FILENAME
The acceptance path must not depend on the agent already knowing an internal filename. Filenames may be canonical destinations, but discovery begins from user intent or from a resource the agent has already encountered. Avoid instructions equivalent to 'go read obscure/path/file.ext' unless the repository first exposes why that path is the authoritative destination for the selected use case.

REVERSE-OWNERSHIP QUESTIONS
When an agent lands on a participating script, manifest, validator, prompt, workflow, or capability record, the routing system must let it answer:
- Why does this resource exist?
- What capability or supported use case owns it?
- What user intent leads here?
- What other resources participate in the same path?
- What validator, artifact, or evidence proves the path works?

If one of those answers requires guessing, the reverse route is incomplete. Repair the smallest canonical owner rather than pasting explanatory prose into every implementation file.

FAILURE MODES TO REJECT
- giant indexes that embed every workflow or skill;
- docs-only hooks with no executable or machine-checkable owner where the repository supports one;
- new prompt identities that duplicate an existing canonical route;
- multiple capabilities claiming the same primary use case without explicit precedence;
- orphan scripts or validators that cannot identify their owning route;
- trigger aliases that point to stale or nonexistent IDs;
- circular links that never reach implementation or proof;
- a route that works only because the implementing agent already knew the repository layout.

PROVE BOTH DIRECTIONS
Add or extend the closest routing validator/regression. At minimum exercise two representative traversals:
A. INTENT-FIRST: give a fresh-agent fixture only the desired use case. Prove it reaches the canonical capability, workflow/skill, implementation, expected artifact, and validator without a pre-supplied implementation filename.
B. IMPLEMENTATION-FIRST: begin from one participating implementation-side resource. Prove it resolves back to the owning capability and originating intent, then reaches the related participants and proof.

Fail closed on broken IDs, unresolved links, duplicate primary ownership, or a route that terminates before proof. Keep evidence versioned to the exact repository head and rerun affected traversal proof if routing owners move.

DELIVER
Report the use case, canonical routing owner, forward route, reverse route, files or registry records changed, focused validator/test, representative traversal results, unresolved ambiguity if any, and commit/PR/integration state. Keep the report compact. The success condition is that the repository guides the next agent to the right place without requiring the explanation again.

prompts.name: Lua Flagging + Host Enforcement Repair Loop
prompts.sprintRole: Build or harden a Lua inspection layer plus host-language enforcement and iterative repair loop for agent-generated commands
prompts.useWhen: Agents are emitting brittle, malformed, wrong-shell, unsafe, or non-portable shell/command snippets and the repository needs Lua to classify defects while the host language raises, blocks, cleans up, and drives repair passes before user escalation.
prompts.inspectFirst: Repository governance; current Lua embedding/readiness skill and contract if present; command generators and canonical launchers; shell/platform/profile routing; host-language entrypoints; command-envelope validators; representative bad snippets and valid controls; tests, logs, and escalation boundaries.
prompts.expectedOutput: A reused or repaired Lua/host boundary with structured Lua findings, host-owned blocking/raising and cleanup semantics, representative bad/valid command fixtures, repeated scan/repair/revalidate passes, executable regression proof, and an exact user-only gate only when agent-capable repair is exhausted.
prompts.nextStep: Run the strongest representative bad command through the Lua checker and host enforcement path, repair the first escaped defect class, rerun the valid controls and adjacent cases, and continue until the bounded fixed point or a genuine user-only gate.
prompts.proofGate: Lua only detects/classifies and returns structured findings; the host validates those findings and owns raising/blocking, process control, cleanup/rollback, and exit propagation; blocking findings and checker failures fail closed; at least one deliberate second-pass review exercises adjacent defects plus valid counterexamples; agent-capable repairs are iterated before user escalation; and static proof is never inflated into live execution proof.
prompts.copyContent:
BUILD OR HARDEN A LUA-FLAGGED, HOST-ENFORCED COMMAND SAFETY LOOP. DO NOT TREAT LUA AS THE PROCESS OWNER, AND DO NOT SEND A BAD AGENT-GENERATED COMMAND TO THE USER JUST BECAUSE ONE VALIDATOR PASS COMPLETED.

Repo: xyz_repo_or_path
Agent command surface: xyz_agent_command_surface
Host language/runtime: resolve from the product and repository; do not assume one.
Representative bad command or incident: xyz_bad_command_or_incident

MISSION
Catch brittle, malformed, wrong-shell, unsafe, or non-portable agent-generated commands before execution or user handoff. Reuse the repository's existing Lua embedding/readiness contract when one exists. Lua owns dynamic inspection and structured flagging; the host language owns validation of Lua results, raising/blocking behavior, retries, cleanup/rollback, execution authority, and the final decision to continue or escalate.

ARCHITECTURE BOUNDARY — HOST STAYS IN CONTROL
- Read the current Lua/host contract first. In Triage-compatible repositories, prefer the existing `lua-embedding-readiness` doctrine rather than inventing a second Lua architecture.
- Lua detects and classifies command defects. It returns structured findings; it does not own the host main loop, process lifetime, native side effects, rollback, or critical cleanup.
- The host language validates the finding schema and raises or returns the repository-native typed failure/nonzero result for blocking findings. A Lua error, malformed Lua result, or checker failure is itself a host-visible validation failure; never silently treat it as PASS.
- Keep the Lua sandbox default-deny. Do not grant shell, filesystem, network, OS, native-module, or arbitrary host-call access merely so the checker can inspect text.
- Do not pretend a Lua runtime or host adapter exists when repository evidence says it is only designed or partially implemented. Build contracts, fixtures, validators, and a product-lane implementation only where current scope and runtime support it.

STRUCTURED FLAG CONTRACT
Reuse an existing schema if present. Otherwise define the smallest versioned result shape needed by the host, with fields equivalent to:
- rule_id
- severity
- category
- shell_or_language
- location or span
- evidence
- host_action
- remediation_hint
- retryable
Keep the contract deterministic and machine-readable. The host must reject unknown required shapes, impossible severities, or malformed findings rather than guessing.

COMMAND CLASSES TO EXERCISE
Derive rules from repository doctrine and real incidents instead of inventing a universal shell style guide. Include representative fixtures where applicable for:
- wrong-shell syntax, such as Bash constructs emitted for a PowerShell or CMD operator path;
- quoting, escaping, interpolation, command-substitution, pipe, redirection, and multiline defects;
- platform/path assumptions that contradict the selected execution profile;
- swallowed or unpropagated exit codes and failure conditions;
- unbounded destructive or broad mutation commands where repository policy requires a bounded form;
- commands that bypass canonical launchers, guards, manifests, or safe wrappers without evidence;
- partial snippets that cannot satisfy the requested operation as written;
- valid counterexamples that resemble risky syntax but are correct in the declared shell.
Do not turn subjective style preferences into blocking rules. Every blocking rule needs an evidence-backed failure mode and at least one valid counterexample where practical.

HOST ENFORCEMENT
For each Lua finding, define the host behavior explicitly:
- PASS: continue only when the structured result is valid and no blocking finding exists.
- WARN: preserve the diagnostic and continue only when repository policy permits.
- BLOCK: prevent execution/handoff, raise the native host failure, preserve rule ID/evidence/remediation context, and return control to the repair loop.
- CHECKER_FAILURE: fail closed in the host with a distinct diagnostic; do not reinterpret validator failure as a clean command.
The host owns cleanup, rollback, timeout, resource release, exit-code propagation, and durable evidence. Lua reports policy findings; the host enforces them.

MULTI-PASS REPAIR LOOP
Run deliberate bounded passes:
SCAN -> LUA FLAGS -> HOST BLOCK/RAISE -> AGENT REPAIR -> REVALIDATE.
Pass 1 must reproduce the representative bad command and prove that Lua flags it and the host refuses it.
Pass 2 must inspect the repaired command plus nearby failure classes and valid controls. Do not stop because the originally observed string changed.
Continue until a bounded fixed point: no practical blocking finding, malformed checker output, missed applicable failure class, broken valid control, or safe in-scope improvement is exposed by current evidence.
If a repair creates a new flag, consume that evidence in the next pass. Never weaken the Lua rule, host exception, fixture, or validator merely to obtain green output.
Record the flag set and disposition by pass so later agents can tell what was caught, repaired, superseded, or intentionally allowed.

AGENT AUTONOMY / USER-ONLY GATE
Keep agent-capable work with the agent. Inspect code, fixtures, shell/profile contracts, tests, validators, logs, and generated command artifacts yourself. Repair and rerun checks yourself when tools and authority permit.
Do not ask the user to choose between technically equivalent safe implementations, copy diagnostics between tools, inspect files the agent can read, or manually validate a command the agent can test safely.
Escalate only when progress truly requires user-controlled credentials, protected or physical runtime access, explicit authorization/consent, an irreducible product preference, or another action the agent cannot perform. When escalation is necessary, present the exact surviving flag/gate, what has already been tried, and the smallest concrete user action that unlocks the next pass.

VALIDATION
Use the strongest safe layers available:
1. schema/contract validation for Lua findings;
2. Lua checker fixtures and negative/positive cases;
3. host-language tests proving BLOCK and CHECKER_FAILURE become real host failures and PASS remains runnable;
4. shell/profile-specific syntax or parser checks where available;
5. integration tests proving generated command -> Lua inspection -> host enforcement -> repair/retry;
6. live/runtime proof only when explicitly authorized and necessary.
Do not claim command safety from Lua-only tests when the host raise/block path is untested. Do not claim live execution proof from static parsing.

DELIVER
Implement or repair the smallest canonical Lua/host enforcement surface rather than adding a competing checker. Report:
- existing architecture owner reused;
- Lua flag schema/rules;
- host enforcement mapping;
- representative bad and valid fixtures;
- repair passes and findings closed;
- tests/validators actually run;
- files, commits, PR/integration state;
- proof level and proof ceiling;
- remaining user-only gate, if any.
A green result is valid only when the Lua detector and host raiser agree on the same command outcome and the bounded repair loop has completed a deliberate second-pass review.

prompts.name: Failure-Class Generalization & Repository Audit
prompts.sprintRole: Generalize a proven defect into a failure-state class, audit analogous repository boundaries, repair reachable instances, and prove adjacent states rather than only the reported input
prompts.useWhen: A real defect, crash, field discrepancy, or suspicious boundary was found and fixing the exact symptom may leave neighboring states or analogous code paths untested.
prompts.inspectFirst: The reproduced defect and its evidence; owning implementation; nearby tests; analogous native/process, parsing, filesystem, state, network, privilege, serialization, cleanup, retry, upgrade, and concurrency boundaries; current validators and production entrypoints.
prompts.expectedOutput: A named failure class, bounded state matrix, repository-wide candidate audit with false positives rejected, repaired practical occurrences, focused regressions for the observed and nearest meaningful adjacent states, and exact remaining proof gaps.
prompts.nextStep: Reproduce the defect, name the failure class, build the smallest applicable state matrix, search for analogous reachable boundaries, repair proven gaps, and rerun the matrix until no practical adjacent state remains unproved.
prompts.proofGate: The reported defect is reproduced or otherwise evidence-backed; the failure class and applicable neighboring states are explicit; analogous candidates are inspected rather than blindly rewritten; observed plus nearest meaningful success/empty/null/malformed/partial/failure/retry/upgrade states are tested where applicable; and remaining unknowns are not called closed.
prompts.copyContent:
GENERALIZE THE FIELD FAILURE. FIX THE CLASS, NOT ONLY THE STRING THAT FAILED.

Repo: xyz_repo_or_path
Observed defect/evidence: xyz_defect_or_incident
Affected entrypoint: xyz_entrypoint_if_known

MISSION
Turn one real defect into a bounded failure-class audit. Reproduce or evidence the defect, identify the underlying boundary assumption, enumerate the nearest meaningful states that share that assumption, search the repository for analogous reachable instances, repair proven gaps, and add regressions that close the class without cargo-cult rewrites.

1. START FROM EVIDENCE
- Preserve the exact failing input, stack/error, runtime, shell/interpreter, platform, state, and entrypoint when available.
- Distinguish root cause from surface symptom. Name the assumption that failed: null/empty handling, process-output contract, locale parsing, path/environment assumption, partial write, stale state, retry/idempotency, cleanup masking, upgrade transition, privilege/context, network transition, serialization drift, concurrency, or another evidence-backed class.
- Do not invent a universal checklist. Select only states plausible for this boundary.

2. BUILD A FAILURE-STATE MATRIX
For the selected class, include the nearest meaningful cells. Typical cells are:
- ordinary success;
- empty or null success;
- malformed or unexpected shape;
- partial/interrupted result;
- ordinary failure;
- silent failure or missing diagnostics;
- retry/re-entry/idempotent repeat;
- old-state -> new-state upgrade;
- concurrent or privilege/context variant when relevant.
Mark each cell PROVED, FAILING, NOT APPLICABLE, or UNKNOWN. UNKNOWN is not PASS.

3. AUDIT ANALOGOUS REPOSITORY BOUNDARIES
Search for the dangerous idiom or assumption across the repository. Examples: direct dereference after native commands, nullable `.Trim()`/property access, optional JSON fields, unchecked registry/environment reads, locale-sensitive parsing, partial-state cleanup, stale cache/state, unchecked exit codes.
For every candidate: inspect reachability and contract before mutation. Reject false positives explicitly. Do not blanket-replace syntax merely because it resembles the incident.

4. REPAIR + REGRESS
- Fix the smallest canonical owner for each proven reachable gap.
- Add the observed failure as a regression.
- Add the nearest meaningful adjacent cells that would fail for the same reason.
- Preserve valid counterexamples so the fix does not over-block legitimate behavior.
- If the class crosses components, add integration proof at the actual boundary, not only helper-unit coverage.

5. SECOND PASS
After green tests, inspect the diff and matrix again. Ask: `What adjacent state could still fail for the same underlying reason?` Search once more for analogous reachable occurrences. Convert concrete gaps into another repair pass. Do not manufacture churn when the bounded matrix is actually closed.

6. AUTONOMY
Run searches, tests, fixtures, validators, and safe repairs yourself. Do not send the user hunting for code or reproducing checks the agent can perform. Escalate only a genuine user-only credential, protected runtime, physical action, authorization, or irreducible product decision.

DELIVER
Report: observed defect; failure class; state matrix and dispositions; analogous candidates inspected; repairs; regressions; tests run; proof ceiling; remaining UNKNOWN cells; commit/PR/integration state.

CLOSURE RULE
A test proving the reported input is fixed is necessary, not sufficient. Close the defect class only when the nearest practical adjacent states and reachable analogues are either proved, repaired, not applicable with evidence, or explicitly left as gaps.

prompts.name: Production-Path Proof Gap Auditor
prompts.sprintRole: Compare the real operator or production execution path with the tested path boundary-by-boundary, expose bypassed assumptions, and close practical proof gaps
prompts.useWhen: Tests are green but a field or production path still fails, or confidence depends on helpers that may bypass launchers, shells, native processes, privileges, state transitions, upgrades, or other real execution boundaries.
prompts.inspectFirst: The real user/operator entrypoint; launchers/wrappers; shell/interpreter and platform; environment and configuration; network/auth/privilege context; filesystem/state/cache; native-process boundaries; serialization; cleanup/retry/upgrade behavior; current tests and CI paths.
prompts.expectedOutput: A production-vs-test path map, explicit unproved production-only boundaries, strengthened integration or entrypoint tests, repaired path mismatches where found, and a proof ceiling that distinguishes helper green from real-path proof.
prompts.nextStep: Trace the production entrypoint and strongest current test side-by-side, identify the first boundary present in production but absent or simulated in test, reproduce or instrument it, then repair and rerun through the same entrypoint.
prompts.proofGate: The real production/operator path and test path are mapped in order; every material production-only boundary is proved, repaired, marked not applicable with evidence, or reported UNKNOWN; at least one strongest-safe same-entrypoint check runs where possible; and helper/unit success is never promoted to production-path proof by assumption.
prompts.copyContent:
AUDIT THE REAL EXECUTION PATH, NOT JUST THE GREEN TEST PATH.

Repo: xyz_repo_or_path
User/production entrypoint: xyz_real_entrypoint
Current green proof: xyz_tests_or_ci
Observed field gap, if any: xyz_incident_or_unknown

MISSION
Find where production behavior can diverge from test behavior. Trace the real operator path and the strongest current test path side-by-side, boundary by boundary. Close practical gaps with the smallest integration, entrypoint, fixture, or implementation repair. Do not treat a helper test as proof of a wrapper, shell, native process, privilege, state transition, upgrade, or runtime it bypasses.

1. MAP BOTH PATHS
Write the ordered path for:
A. REAL: user action -> launcher/wrapper -> shell/interpreter -> configuration/environment -> auth/network/privilege -> filesystem/state -> native processes/services -> serialization/output -> cleanup/restore.
B. TEST: test runner -> fixtures/mocks/helpers -> exercised boundaries -> assertions.
Use repository evidence. Do not invent production components.

2. DIFF THE BOUNDARIES
For each real-path boundary, mark:
- SAME + PROVED;
- SAME + WEAKER INPUT;
- SIMULATED/MOCKED;
- BYPASSED;
- PRODUCTION-ONLY;
- UNKNOWN.
Pay special attention to launch scripts, shell differences, Windows/POSIX behavior, native stdout/stderr/exit codes, paths and environment variables, network state, credentials/authority, user vs SYSTEM/admin context, filesystem permissions, stale/generated state, first-run vs repeat-run, old-runtime -> new-runtime refresh, retries, cleanup/finally, and serialization/schema drift. Only include boundaries relevant to the product.

3. ATTACK THE FIRST MATERIAL GAP
Choose the earliest practical boundary where production has weaker proof than tests. Reproduce it safely, add instrumentation/fixture coverage, or run the actual entrypoint in a bounded environment. If the boundary exposes a defect, repair the canonical owner and rerun from the entrypoint.

4. PROOF LADDER
Label evidence accurately:
- static/schema proof;
- helper/unit proof;
- component integration proof;
- same-entrypoint synthetic proof;
- live/runtime proof.
Never skip levels in the report. Green helper tests do not prove a production wrapper they never invoked. Static parse does not prove native runtime semantics.

5. SECOND PASS
After the first gap closes, remap both paths from the current head. Ask which real boundary is still bypassed, mocked differently, state-sensitive, or upgrade-sensitive. Continue through practical gaps until the remaining differences are proved, truly not applicable, or exact blockers.

6. AUTONOMOUS EXECUTION
Inspect launchers, tests, CI, logs, fixtures, and runtime-safe paths yourself. Run safe entrypoint checks yourself. Do not ask the user to become the test runner or log bridge. Escalate only for credentials, protected/live runtime access, physical action, explicit authorization, or another genuinely inaccessible gate.

DELIVER
Report: production path; test path; boundary diff; gaps found/closed; exact tests and entrypoints run; defects repaired; proof level/ceiling; remaining UNKNOWN/blocked boundaries; commit/PR/integration state.

CLOSURE RULE
A green suite is not enough when it bypasses a material production boundary. Close only when the real path has no practical unaccounted boundary at the claimed proof level.

prompts.name: Use-Case Closure Certification
prompts.sprintRole: Reconstruct a user-facing closure claim into acceptance obligations, try to falsify it, repair exposed gaps, and certify only evidence-backed closure
prompts.useWhen: A feature, workflow, deployment, or operator use case is being called done/working/closed and the claim needs adversarial acceptance proof rather than a completion summary.
prompts.inspectFirst: The original user-facing request and closure claim; current implementation and entrypoints; acceptance criteria; tests/validators; generated artifacts; known incidents; first-run/repeat-run/failure/upgrade/context variants; integration and runtime evidence.
prompts.expectedOutput: A reconstructed closure claim, obligation ledger with PASS/FAIL/UNKNOWN/NOT-APPLICABLE states, adversarial falsification attempts, repaired in-scope gaps, rerun proof, and an exact certified proof level or reason closure remains open.
prompts.nextStep: Translate the user-facing claim into concrete observable obligations, mark current evidence without treating unknown as pass, attack the weakest obligation, repair any exposed gap, and repeat until the claim survives the bounded falsification pass.
prompts.proofGate: Every material obligation implied by the claimed use case is explicit and evidence-linked; UNKNOWN is not PASS; at least one deliberate falsification pass covers practical first-run/repeat/failure/upgrade/context variants; exposed in-scope gaps are repaired and revalidated; and certification states the exact proof level without inflating static or synthetic evidence into live closure.

prompts.name: Regression Test & Live Behavior Guard
prompts.sprintRole: Prove that a change preserves previously accepted behavior while adding or repairing the requested behavior, using impact-guided automated regressions plus canonical live tests when the claim is runtime-facing
prompts.useWhen: A code, configuration, migration, refactor, bug fix, or feature change may break behavior that previously worked, especially when agents are tempted to validate only the new happy path or the tests they just edited.
prompts.inspectFirst: Current default-branch fixed point; exact changed head/diff; original user outcome and prior accepted behavior; existing tests and runtime evidence; callers/call stacks/interfaces/contracts/state boundaries touched by the change; incidents and regressions; canonical launchers/entrypoints; safe live-test environment and proof limits. For interactive products, inspect multi-step keyboard/pointer sequences and the ownership of search, filters, focus, selection, panel, clipboard, notification, and preference state rather than testing each control in isolation.
prompts.expectedOutput: A protected-behavior ledger, change-impact/call-stack map, before/after regression evidence, new and existing automated tests, canonical live behavior proof when safely available, repaired regressions, deliberate second-pass review, and an honest proof ceiling for any runtime that cannot be exercised. For UI changes, include sequence-level controls proving orthogonal state survives unrelated actions and that a repaired shortcut reaches its intended terminal action without creating a new redundant interaction.
prompts.nextStep: Pin the known-good fixed point and changed head, derive the smallest protected-behavior set from accepted behavior and impacted call stacks, run baseline/current tests plus the canonical live path where safe, repair any regression without weakening the old contract, then rerun both old and new behavior through a second pass.
prompts.proofGate: Previously accepted behavior is explicit rather than inferred from the changed tests alone; impacted callers/call stacks and state/contracts are inspected; expected outputs are not rewritten merely to bless a regression; both requested behavior and protected controls pass; runtime-facing claims receive canonical live proof when safely executable or an exact runtime blocker/proof ceiling; and a deliberate second pass finds no practical untested regression surface in scope. Interactive regressions include realistic action sequences: controls preserve state they do not semantically own, and keyboard/pointer routes that mean the same thing converge on equivalent observable results.
prompts.copyContent:
